Oxidation happens at the anode, so first discard anything written as a reduction.
(A) Na⁺ + e⁻ ⇒ Na and (C) H⁺ + e⁻ ⇒ ½H₂ both gain electrons — these are cathode reactions.
That leaves two possible oxidations, water and chloride:
2H₂O ⇒ O₂ + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻, E° = 1.23 V
2Cl⁻ ⇒ Cl₂ + 2e⁻, E° = 1.36 V
On the numbers alone water should win, since the lower potential is easier to oxidise.
In practice chlorine is what comes off, because the oxygen evolution reaction has a large
overpotential on the electrode — it needs several tenths of a volt more than its E° suggests.
With concentrated brine that overpotential more than wipes out the 0.13 V gap.
This is why the chlor-alkali industry gets Cl₂ and NaOH from brine rather than O₂.
∴ Cl⁻ ⇒ ½Cl₂ + e⁻ occurs at the anode.
kcet|Chemistry|2017|27||0|0:
The Arrhenius equation is k = Ae^(−Ea/RT), and the rate follows k.
Raising T makes the exponent −Ea/RT less negative, so e^(−Ea/RT) grows and k grows with it.
The dependence is exponential, which is why a 10 K rise often roughly doubles the rate.
(A) says exactly this ✓
(C) is the reverse of it — k rises with temperature, it does not fall, so (C) is wrong.
(D) is wrong too: Ea sits in the exponent, so changing it certainly changes the rate.
(Note (B), rate rises as Ea falls, is also true of the equation — it is what a catalyst exploits —
but the official key marks (A), the temperature dependence the equation is usually quoted for.)
∴ the rate of a reaction increases with increase in temperature.
kcet|Chemistry|2017|28||0|0:
The question asks for the statement that is false.
(B) True — reactions that go in several steps often show fractional orders, because the observed
rate law comes from the slowest step and any pre-equilibria before it.
(C) True — bimolecular means two species must meet in a single collision event.
(D) True — molecularity counts the species colliding in one elementary step, so it has no meaning
for an overall reaction built from several steps.
(A) False — a rate law can only ever be found by experiment. You cannot read it off the balanced
equation; the orders have to be measured, for example by the initial rate method, holding one
concentration fixed and varying another.
That is the whole distinction between order (experimental) and stoichiometry (from the equation).
∴ statement (A) is the incorrect one.

kcet|Chemistry|2017|29||0|0.s:
For a reaction aA ⇒ bB the single rate of reaction is defined by dividing each rate by its
stoichiometric coefficient:
rate = −(1/a)·d[A]/dt = (1/b)·d[B]/dt
Here the equation is ½A ⇒ 2B, so a = ½ and b = 2.
−(1/½)·d[A]/dt = (1/2)·d[B]/dt
−2·d[A]/dt = (1/2)·d[B]/dt
Divide both sides by 2:
−d[A]/dt = (1/4)·d[B]/dt
Sanity check: B is produced with a coefficient four times that of A (2 against ½), so B must
appear four times as fast as A disappears ✓
∴ −d[A]/dt = ¼·d[B]/dt.

kcet|Chemistry|2017|30||0|0:
River water carries clay and silt as a negatively charged colloidal sol, kept dispersed because
the like charges on the particles repel each other.
Sea water is full of electrolyte — mainly Na⁺, Mg²⁺ and Ca²⁺.
When the two meet, these positive ions neutralise the charge on the clay particles.
The repulsion that kept them apart disappears, so they clump together and settle out.
That deposition builds the delta.
This is coagulation, and by the Hardy–Schulze rule the higher the charge on the added cation
the more effective it is, so Mg²⁺ and Ca²⁺ do more of the work than Na⁺.
(B) colloid formation is the opposite process, and (D) peptization disperses a precipitate back
into a sol — again the reverse.
∴ coagulation.

kcet|Chemistry|2017|31||0|0.s:
Classify by the phases present.
Vegetable oil is a liquid, hydrogen is a gas, and finely divided nickel is a solid.
The catalyst is therefore in a different phase from the reactants, which is the definition of
heterogeneous catalysis.
The reaction happens on the metal's surface: H₂ is adsorbed and its H–H bond weakened,
the C=C of the oil adsorbs alongside it, and hydrogen adds across the double bond.
This is why the nickel is 'finely divided' — the catalysis is a surface effect, so the greater the
surface area the faster it goes.
The product is the saturated solid fat, which is how vanaspati is made.
Homogeneous catalysis (B) would need the catalyst in the same phase, as in acid-catalysed
ester hydrolysis.
∴ heterogeneous catalysis.
